chunks: "The input current of an LDO is the output current plus the regulator's own quiescent current, and the input voltage is V in , so efficiency is V outI out divided by V in(I out plus I Q) .
If the load current is much bigger than I Q , that's just V out over V in . So output current and dropout affect it in different ways.
In the middle of the range, load current doesn't change efficiency at all, it's set by the voltage ratio.
At very light load, I Q matters: when I out is equal to I Q , efficiency is half of V out over V in .
A 50 microamps part with a 10 microamps load is down to about 17% of the ideal. Dropout shows up at the other end.
The dropout voltage is roughly load current times R DS(on) , so a higher current needs more headroom.
If the input is set at the minimum, V out plus I R DS(on) , the best efficiency is V out over (V out plus V DO) : 94% for 3.
3 volts with 200 millivolts dropout, but only 80% at 2 amps if the resistance is 0. 4 ohms. And if the input goes below that point, the LDO is out of regulation entirely.
So to maximize LDO efficiency I'd keep V in as close to V out plus V DO as the worst case allows, and choose a part whose I Q is small compared with my lightest load."
